The easy image gets a single-class set; the moderate image gets a few alternatives; the hard image's set contains many similar-looking species, and the ground truth ranks second rather than first. In *A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification* [[1]](#ref-1) (arXiv preprint, July 2021; later published in *Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning*, 2023), [Anastasios N. Angelopoulos](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~angelopoulos/) and [Stephen Bates](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=LeshmV8AAAAJ) (Berkeley) walk through conformal prediction as a hands-on, code-first recipe for turning any black-box model into one whose predictions come with a distribution-free coverage guarantee.

> Black-box machine learning models are now routinely used in high-risk settings, like medical diagnostics, which demand uncertainty quantification to avoid consequential model failures. *Conformal prediction* is a user-friendly paradigm for creating statistically rigorous uncertainty sets/intervals for the predictions of such models. Critically, the sets are *valid in a distribution-free sense: they possess explicit, non-asymptotic guarantees even without distributional assumptions or model assumptions*. One can use conformal prediction with *any pre-trained model*, such as a neural network, to produce sets that are *guaranteed to contain the ground truth with a user-specified probability, such as 90%*. It is easy-to-understand, easy-to-use, and general, applying naturally to problems arising in the fields of computer vision, natural language processing, deep reinforcement learning, and so on. This hands-on introduction is aimed to provide the reader a working understanding of conformal prediction and related distribution-free uncertainty quantification techniques with one self-contained document. We lead the reader through practical theory for and examples of conformal prediction and describe its extensions to complex machine learning tasks involving structured outputs, distribution shift, time-series, outliers, models that abstain, and more. Throughout, there are many explanatory illustrations, examples, and code samples in Python. With each code sample comes a Jupyter notebook implementing the method on a real-data example; the notebooks can be accessed and easily run using our codebase.

This post doubles as standing background for the blog's posts on [conformal language modeling](/posts/20260505-conformal-language-modeling/), [conformal factuality](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/), and related calibration work.

## What conformal prediction is

Conformal prediction [[1]](#ref-1), [[2]](#ref-2) is a distribution-free statistical framework that turns any predictor into one that outputs *sets* with a calibrated coverage guarantee. Given a trained model and a labeled *calibration set* not used in training, score each calibration example with some non-conformity function (for example, $1 - p(y_i \mid x_i)$ for classification), take the $(1-\epsilon)$-quantile of those scores, and at test time return every candidate whose score falls below that quantile. If the calibration and test data are [exchangeable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchangeable_random_variables), the returned set contains the true label with probability at least $1-\epsilon$, without assumptions about the model's own calibration or the data distribution. The framework dates to the late 1990s (Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer) and is a standard tool for uncertainty quantification outside deep learning.

The recipe is three steps, and the paper lays them out alongside matching Python: compute non-conformity scores on the calibration data; read off the calibration quantile $\hat{q}$; build the test-time set from every class whose score falls below $\hat{q}$.

![The conformal recipe in three steps: (1) compute non-conformity scores on held-out calibration data, where the score is one minus the softmax output of the true class; (2) take $\hat{q}$, the $\lceil(n+1)(1-\epsilon)\rceil/n$ empirical quantile of those scores; (3) at test time, return every class whose score falls below $\hat{q}$. Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure2.png){fig-align="center"}

The guarantee is exact and two-sided. For a calibration set of size $n$, the coverage of the returned set $\mathcal{C}(X_{\text{test}})$ obeys

$$1-\epsilon \;\le\; \mathbb{P}\big(Y_{\text{test}} \in \mathcal{C}(X_{\text{test}})\big) \;\le\; 1-\epsilon+\frac{1}{n+1},$$

a result the paper attributes to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders. It holds for any $n$, so the floor of $1-\epsilon$ is met even with a small calibration set, and the upper bound shows the procedure does not badly over-cover.

## A concrete CIFAR-10 walkthrough

Take a CIFAR-10 image classifier with softmax outputs and target $\epsilon = 0.1$. On 1,000 held-out calibration images, score each by $s_i = 1 - p(y_i \mid x_i)$ (one minus the model's probability on the true class). Sort the 1,000 scores in ascending order and take the 901st value (the $\lceil 0.9 \cdot 1001 \rceil$-th); call it $\hat{q}$. On a new test image $x$, return the set of classes $\{y : 1 - p(y \mid x) \leq \hat{q}\}$. When the test image comes from the same distribution as calibration, the returned *set* contains the correct class at least 90% of the time. This is a weaker claim than "the top-1 prediction is correct 90% of the time" — a set of all 10 classes trivially contains the truth yet conveys no information. Depending on difficulty, the set might contain one class (easy image), three or four (moderate), or all ten (a hard image the model has no clear read on). The number of distinct classes in the set is how conformal prediction communicates uncertainty, widening on harder inputs.

## Two knobs control set size

At a given coverage level, two knobs determine how big the returned set ends up. Smaller $\epsilon$ demands tighter coverage, pushes the calibration quantile into the right tail, and forces $\hat{q}$ up, so more candidates pass the test-time filter. At the extreme $\epsilon < 1/(n+1)$, where $n$ is the calibration set size, the quantile is undefined and the set becomes "everything," which satisfies the guarantee trivially but is uninformative.

Model quality is the second knob. A better predictor assigns higher probability to the true class on calibration points, giving smaller non-conformity scores, a lower $\hat{q}$, and a stricter probability floor at test time. Because a better model still puts enough mass on the correct class to clear that stricter floor, it produces sharper sets at the same $\epsilon$. Weaker models hit the same coverage but through larger, less informative sets. Set size then doubles as a data-driven measure of model quality pegged to a formal guarantee.

## Ranking drives the guarantee

One subtlety worth naming: conformal prediction uses score *rankings*, and the coverage guarantee does not require the model's probabilities to be calibrated. Any monotone-in-relevance scoring function works, because the quantile adapts to whatever the calibration scores look like. The cost of miscalibration shows up in set size rather than coverage: a rank-destroying miscalibration inflates $\hat{q}$ and dilates the set, but the $(1-\epsilon)$ guarantee still holds.

## The returned set is a coverage hull

This means the returned set is a coverage hull. It does not convey relative likelihoods across elements, calibrated per-candidate confidences, or any distributional information beyond "at least one of these is correct at the chosen $\epsilon$." If a downstream consumer needs to know which answer in the set is most likely, conformal prediction leaves that to a separate mechanism, whether a raw ranking used informally or a Bayesian or ensemble method.

## Marginal coverage, not conditional

The guarantee is *marginal*: the probability is averaged over the randomness in both the calibration draw and the test point. It does not promise the same coverage for every input or every subgroup. The paper makes the distinction concrete with three regimes, shown below for a two-group classification problem and a regression band. With no coverage, one group is badly under-covered (5%) while the other does better (14%). Marginal coverage hits the target *on average* but can do it by over-covering one group (100%) and under-covering the other (80%). Only conditional coverage holds the target within each group (90% and 90%) and spreads errors evenly across the input space.

![Three notions of coverage at a 90% target. Top row: errors by group, with green points correctly covered and red points missed. Bottom row: the same idea for a regression band. No coverage misses the target; marginal coverage meets it on average but lets errors concentrate in one group or region; conditional coverage holds the target within every group. Figure 10 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure10.png){fig-align="center"}

Conditional coverage is what most deployments actually want, and split-conformal prediction does not deliver it. Adaptivity — letting set size grow on genuinely harder inputs — is the practical proxy the paper recommends measuring, since the marginal guarantee says nothing about whether hard and easy inputs are treated differently.

## Why generative LMs are harder

The framework above assumes a finite candidate set you can enumerate (the $K$ classes). Generative language models break this assumption: the output space is the combinatorial space of all possible text sequences, so you can't score every candidate. Adapting conformal prediction to LMs requires replacing enumeration with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule. That adaptation is the subject of the [Conformal Language Modeling](/posts/20260505-conformal-language-modeling/) post. A related adaptation, specifically for factual claim verification, is the subject of the [Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/) post.

## My Notes

- **A two-decade-old method, repackaged for deep learning**: conformal prediction's machinery dates to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders in the late 1990s and the 2005 monograph [[2]](#ref-2), which reads as dense measure-theoretic statistics. What this tutorial added was not a new theorem but a packaging: the split-conformal recipe written as a few lines of Python against a frozen neural network, with a runnable notebook per method. That repackaging is most of why conformal prediction moved from a statistics niche into mainstream machine-learning practice rather than staying in the literature it came from.
- **Why conditional coverage is out of reach**: split-conformal settles for marginal coverage because the conditional version most deployments want is provably unreachable. Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani [[3]](#ref-3) prove that any distribution-free method with nontrivial conditional coverage must return uninformative (effectively infinite-width) sets. So marginal coverage isn't a shortcoming of this particular recipe. It's the strongest promise any assumption-free method can make. The [conformal factuality](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/) post flags the same caveat from the deployment side: a per-prompt error rate can run well above the calibrated average.
- **Exchangeability is the real assumption**: the guarantee needs calibration and test data to be exchangeable, which is weaker than i.i.d. but still fails under covariate shift and temporal drift, exactly the conditions production models run in. Weighted conformal prediction [[4]](#ref-4) restores coverage under a *known* covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio between test and calibration distributions, and the conformal-prediction-beyond-exchangeability line [[5]](#ref-5) handles drift with no shift model by down-weighting older calibration points. Both are the natural next reading once the i.i.d. framing here starts to pinch.
